# Essais cliniques et traitements innovants

Tout au long de l'année, des essais cliniques sont mis en œuvre afin d'améliorer la prise en charge des animaux de compagnie. L'EnvA, dans ses cliniques, propose aux propriétaires d'en bénéficier en participant à des études.
Ophtalmologie

Une étude clinique pour un nouveau traitement médical de la cataracte diabétique chez le chien menée à l'hôpital des animaux de compagnie.

 

Une étude est en cours à l'école nationale vétérinaire d'Alfort afin d’optimiser la prise en charge des entéropathies exsudatives, maladie complexe dont le pronostic peut être sombre. Les spécialistes de l'hôpital des animaux de compagnie recrutent des chiens avec entéropathies exsudatives dans le cadre d'une étude afin de mieux comprendre cette affection.

La prise en charge des chiens a donc pour objectif d’améliorer le pronostic en proposant une alimentation ciblée et un suivi régulier.
L'EnvA recrute ainsi tout chien présentant une hypo-albuminémie et/ou des troubles digestifs.

L'étude n'entraine aucun risque supplémentaire pour l'animal et permet un suivi gratuit durant plusieurs semaines.

## Besoin d’aide dans vos recherches?

Trouver un essai clinique peut être une démarche difficile et complexe. C’est pour cela que notre partenaire Q-CROC a mis en place Onco+, un service d’accompagnement gratuit, offert pour toute personne à la recherche d’un essai clinique en oncologie au Québec.

Ce service est offert en collaboration avec la Fondation québécoise du cancer. Une infirmière spécialisée en oncologie de notre Ligne Info-cancer vous aidera personnellement tout au long du processus de recherche d’un essai clinique. Nous assurerons la confidentialité et la sécurité de vos informations.

Dogs and cats develop naturally occurring tumors that closely resemble human malignancies in histopathology, molecular alterations, tumor microenvironments, and treatment response. These species also share exposure to environmental carcinogens and demonstrate conserved pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) profiles of several chemotherapeutic agents. This review provides a comprehensive comparison of cancer epidemiology, tumor biology, pharmacologic treatment modalities, drug formulation challenges, and regulatory considerations in humans, dogs, and cats. Key molecular targets such as TP53, HER2, EGFR, and PD-L1 exhibit cross-species conservation, supporting the relevance of companion animals in biomarker discovery and drug screening.

Comme les humains, les chiens et les chats peuvent développer des cancers ou des tumeurs dans différentes parties de leur corps. Ces dernières années, l’oncologie vétérinaire a connu des avancées rapides. L’augmentation du nombre de cas permet de renforcer notre expérience et notre expertise, et de proposer des techniques de diagnostic et des traitements toujours plus performants (imagerie, analyses de laboratoire, radiothérapie, etc.).

Chez les animaux, les effets secondaires sont généralement moins fréquents et moins marqués que chez l’Homme. Ils peuvent toutefois apparaître et se traduire par une perte d’appétit, des nausées, des vomissements ou de la fatigue. Des traitements adaptés peuvent être mis en place afin de limiter ces effets tout en restant compatibles avec la chimiothérapie.

Chez certains chiens, des rougeurs cutanées peuvent également survenir, entraînant parfois des démangeaisons et du léchage.

Chez les chats, des desquamations peuvent être observées, la peau ayant tendance à s’écailler.

Ces effets secondaires restent généralement modérés et bien pris en charge.

## Quelle est la fréquence du cancer chez les chiens et les chats ?

Bien que n’importe quel chat ou chien puisse avoir le cancer, il est plus fréquent chez les animaux plus âgés. Selon l’American Veterinary Medical Association, les chiens ont à peu près autant de risques que les humains en ce qui concerne le cancer, avec près de la moitié de les chiens gériatriques (ceux de plus de 10 ans) développent un cancer à un moment donné.

UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours
Date: Mon Feb  9 01:00:00 2026 UTC

UQ Gatton Professor Rachel Allavena said the drug Enzistat developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune has the potential to treat cancers in dogs and humans. "It gives dogs in southeast Queensland another option, and it's always nice to do cutting edge trials," she said. "The early data that the company has is that it's helped dogs survive longer and have less bad side effects from their cancer. "We're quite hopeful that for dogs that might not have a lot of options that it might be a useful drug in the future." UQ is looking for 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 dogs in palliative care to be part of the trial. Professor Allavena said they hope the drug can shrink inoperable tumours so they could be removed surgically and give a final hope for dogs in palliative care. "They don't have hope for a cure any other way, but their owners just want to see if they can keep them to be around a little longer and see if it can make them more comfortable," she said. She said a third to a half of dogs will get cancer and it is more common than in lots of other species. Professor Allavena has been researching immune-based cancer therapies for about 15 years and she said it was really hard at times. "It's really hard when we hear about one of our patients passing away," she said. "We do also get a lot of joy from giving people hope or giving the animals options." Anyone interested in joining the trial need a cancer diagnosis and referral from their vet. People involved in the trial would need to give a tablet to their dog twice a day for six weeks and need to come to UQ Gatton three times throughout the trial. The medication and any additional blood tests, biopsies, or examinations are provided as part of the study and owners have to cover any other veterinary costs. Contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au to join the trial.

Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says (https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2026/05/30/scientists-find-cancer-gene-similarities-cats-humans-study-says/)
【turn1040news18】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4 months ago; A recent study led by Louise van der Weyden and international researchers has discovered significant genetic similarities between feline and human cancers, offering promising avenues for shared treatment advancements. Analyzing tumor samples from nearly 500 domestic cats across multiple countries, the researchers identified common mutations in about 1,000 cat genes that correspond to human cancer genes. Among the most striking parallels was the FBXW7 gene, a tumor suppressor found mutated in both feline mammary tumors and human breast cancer, associated with poor prognoses.

Published in the journal Science, the research underlines cats as effective disease models due to their genetic closeness to humans and shared living environments that expose them to similar carcinogens. The study also revealed chemotherapy drug vincristine’s effectiveness in treating feline mammary tumors, providing a potential pathway for clinical trials and the development of targeted treatments. While experts like Jaime Modiano stress that more research is needed, the findings mark a significant step toward dual-species cancer therapy, benefiting both feline and human patients.
Cancer progresses faster in dogs than in people, meaning researchers can receive quicker results with potential treatments in clinical trials with canines. The bone cancer osteosarcoma is more common in dogs than people, so scientists have learned techniques from the animals on how to treat people with the same cancer, and vice versa.
A decade ago, researchers told The Washington Post that dogs were observed more than cats in oncology studies because less was known about feline tumors and cats tended to become more stressed interacting with people.
For their study, van der Weyden and other researchers collected tissue samples from domestic cats from Austria, Canada, England, Germany, New Zealand and Scotland. 
They screened about 1,000 cat genes that are equivalent to human genes associated with cancer. Van der Weyden said she worried they might not find similarities between cat and human cancers, partly because few cat genetic studies had been completed. 
However, in addition to the gene associated with breast cancer in both species, researchers said they found similarities in human and cat cancers affecting their blood, bones, lungs, skin, gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system.
"I was first of all doing it for the cat," said van der Weyden, senior staff scientist at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, a genomics research center in Cambridgeshire, England. "But then to find that there are similarities and we can help humans, that's fantastic."
Researchers found that the chemotherapy drug vincristine was effective against cats' mammary tumors, according to the study, which was published in February. They said that finding could guide veterinary pharmaceutical companies in developing treatment for mammary cancer, which is the third-most-common feline cancer and is typically deadly, according to Cornell University's Feline Health Center.
"Before we just didn't know; we didn't know what drug you could potentially pick," said Wood, who teaches pathology at the University of Guelph in Ontario. "And now there's sort of a list, at least, that could then proceed to clinical trials."
Jaime Modiano, a professor at the University of Minnesota's school of veterinary medicine who was not involved in the research, said the study is a foundation for scientists to learn more about cat and human cancers. However, he said, much more research is required to determine whether the findings can lead to treatments for cats - let alone helping with human cancers.
"It's the first step," Modiano said, "in the journey of a thousand miles."

Rescue dog Rosie’s cancer shrinks after world-first mRNA vaccine
Date: Fri Mar 13 09:30:00 2026 UTC

Now the hi-tech teamwork has unleashed an experimental medicine that offers hope to human patients, by using mRNA vaccines in oncology. Abandoned in bushland, eight-year-old Rosie found her forever home with Sydney tech entrepreneur Paul Conyngham, who adopted the staffy-shar pei cross from an animal shelter in 2019 - just in time for pandemic lockdowns. Heartbroken when his fur-baby was diagnosed with a deadly mast cell cancer in 2024, Mr ­Conyngham threw thousands of dollars at veterinary chemotherapy and surgery, which slowed but failed to shrink the tumours. Now, after treatment with a custom mRNA cancer vaccine over the Christmas break, the tennis ball-sized tumour on Rosie's hock has shrunk in half, in a recovery that has astounded researchers at the cutting-edge of human cancer treatments. "It was like holy crap, it worked!'' says Martin Smith, an associate professor of computational biology and director of the Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics at the University of NSW. "It raises the question, if we can do this for a dog, why aren't we rolling this out to all humans with cancer? It gives hope to a lot of people, and it's something we're passionate about trying to chase up here.'' 'We often get oddball queries' In a tale of tenacity, Mr Conyngham used a chatbot to brainstorm possible cures for Rosie's cancer - then harnessed artificial intelligence to process gigabytes of genetic data to create the blueprint for an mRNA vaccine. How Sydney tech entrepreneur, Paul Conyngham, used artificial intelligence to create the world's first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, achieving remarkable tumour shrinkage that has astounded leading scientists. Harnessing some of Australia's most sought-after scientists to manufacture the vaccine in laboratories at the University of NSW, he then tracked down the only veterinary researcher with ethics approval to administer the experimental drug. It was ChatGPT that suggested immunotherapy, pointing Mr Conyngham to the UNSW Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics, where Associate Professor Smith still remembers the "weird" request. "We often get oddball queries, and this one was coming from a private individual looking to sequence his dog,'' he recalls. "DNA sequencing is a way to profile the tumour and identify mutations that might be causing the disease.'' The renowned researcher was reticent. "Usually we don't support direct-to-consumer type DNA sequencing because while generating data for genomics is relatively easy for us, interrogating that data is really hard and challenging,'' he said.

A new cancer treatment for cats could help humans, too (https://www.sfchronicle.com/health/article/human-cat-oral-cancer-treatment-20881627.php)
【turn1040news20】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 1.1 years ago; A new study, published by researchers from UCSF, UC Davis, and the University of Pittsburgh, presents a groundbreaking cancer treatment for cats that may also benefit human patients with head and neck tumors. The therapy targets STAT3, a transcription factor known to be hyperactivated in about 75% of human tumors. Researchers created a DNA-based decoy molecule that inhibits STAT3 by mimicking the genetic sequences it typically binds to, thereby preventing it from triggering cancer-promoting genes.

In a clinical trial involving 20 pet cats with oral cancer, 35% showed tumor shrinkage or stability, with minimal side effects. One cat, Jak, significantly outlived his prognosis, benefiting from the therapy. The decoy treatment was administered intravenously, an improvement over previous versions requiring direct tumor injection.

The findings revealed immune system changes in treated cats, offering potential biomarkers for identifying patients—both feline and human—who may benefit most. With promising results and improved survival rates in responsive cats, researchers are aiming to fund early-phase human trials while continuing feline studies, suggesting possible future cross-species cancer therapies.
A new cancer treatment for cats could help humans, too
Date: Thu Aug 28 15:00:17 2025 UTC

In a study published Thursday, scientists from UCSF, UC Davis and the University of Pittsburgh describe a promising, first of its kind treatment in pet cats with oral cancer. The authors say the approach could benefit people with head and neck tumors, too.
"There are common features of cancer in cats and cancer in humans," said author Jennifer Grandis, a professor in UCSF's Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery. "We can learn from each other."
The new treatment targets the STAT3 transcription factor, a protein that binds specific DNA sequences to affect gene expression. "This transcription factor is hyperactivated in almost three-quarters of human tumors," said author Daniel Johnson, a professor in UCSF's Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery.
Until now, the protein has proven "incredibly difficult to inhibit," Johnson said. "People have been trying to develop drugs against this protein, STAT3, for many years.

【turn1040news21】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; A groundbreaking study led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute has revealed that domestic cats share significant genetic similarities with humans in the development of cancer, offering new avenues for treatment in both species. Researchers analyzed 13 types of feline tumors from nearly 500 cats across five countries by sequencing DNA from cancerous and healthy tissues. They found mutations in about 1,000 genes linked to human cancers, across various tumor types like blood, bone, lung, skin, gastrointestinal, and central nervous system cancers.

One key finding relates to feline breast cancer, where over half showed mutations in the FBXW7 gene—rare in humans but linked to worse outcomes.
